subject: English
description: English modals — can/could (ability), may/might (possibility), must/should (obligation), shall/will (future), would (conditional), need/dare.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: 'You ___ wear a helmet while riding a bike.' (strong obligation, legal requirement)
questions.explanation: MUST = STRONG OBLIGATION; usually rules, laws, or critical requirements. 'You MUST wear a helmet' = legally required. CONTRAST: SHOULD = recommendation/advice ('you should sleep more') — softer than must. WOULD = conditional or polite past ('I would help if I could'); not for present obligation. MIGHT = low possibility ('it might rain'); does not express obligation. COULD = past ability ('I could swim at age 5') or polite request ('could you help?'); not obligation. SUMMARY OF MODAL FUNCTIONS: (1) Permission: may, can, could (polite). (2) Possibility: may, might, could. (3) Ability: can, could. (4) Obligation: must, should, ought to, have to. (5) Future: will, shall. (6) Past habit: used to, would. KEY EXAM TRAP: 'must' vs 'have to' — both express obligation but 'must' is more PERSONAL/INTERNAL ('I must finish this'); 'have to' is EXTERNAL ('I have to attend the meeting'). PYQ FREQUENCY: modal-fill-blanks appear in CGL, IBPS Clerk, RRB English 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Identify the correct modal: 'When I was a child, I ___ run very fast.'
questions.explanation: COULD is the PAST TENSE of CAN (ability). 'When I was a child' indicates PAST time, so 'could' is correct. The sentence describes a past ability. PAST ABILITY EXAMPLES: 'She could swim at age 4', 'He could read fluently by 5'. CAN — present ability: 'I can swim'. WAS/WERE ABLE TO is also used, especially for SPECIFIC past achievements: 'I WAS ABLE TO solve the puzzle' (specific success); but 'I could solve puzzles' (general past ability). SHOULD = advice/recommendation in present/future, NOT past ability. POLITE-REQUEST USE: 'Could you pass the salt?' is more polite than 'Can you pass the salt?'. CONDITIONAL USE: 'If I had time, I could help' (hypothetical present). EXAM TRAP: 'could' vs 'managed to' — when describing ONE specific past success against difficulty, 'managed to' is preferred ('he managed to climb Everest', NOT 'he could climb Everest' — sounds like ability not achievement). PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 modal Qs per SSC CGL.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: '___ I borrow your pen for a moment?' (polite request)
questions.explanation: MAY is the most FORMAL/POLITE modal for asking permission: 'May I borrow your pen?' CAN and COULD are also acceptable but more INFORMAL: 'Can I borrow your pen?' (casual), 'Could I borrow your pen?' (slightly more polite than can). FORMALITY HIERARCHY for permission requests: MAY (most formal) > COULD > CAN (most casual). WILL is for FUTURE tense or REQUESTS (not permission): 'Will you help me?' SHOULD is for ADVICE: 'Should I take an umbrella?' MUST is OBLIGATION: 'I must leave now'. EXAM-FAVOURITE TRAP: 'Can I X?' vs 'May I X?' — strict grammarians say MAY is for permission, CAN is for ability ('I CAN run' = I'm able to). In modern usage CAN is widely accepted for permission, but MAY is preferred in FORMAL writing/exams. INDIA EXAMS: SSC CGL, IBPS, RBI Grade B all prefer MAY for permission in formal contexts. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 polite-request Qs per SSC, IBPS English. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests politeness-formality awareness.

questions.stem: Pick the correct modal: 'It ___ rain tomorrow — the sky looks cloudy.' (showing possibility)
questions.explanation: MIGHT expresses LOW-TO-MODERATE possibility (~40-60% certainty). 'It might rain' = possible but not certain. POSSIBILITY HIERARCHY (low to high): MIGHT (~30-50%) → MAY (~50-60%) → COULD (~50-60%) → SHOULD (~70-80%, expectation) → WILL (~95%+, certainty). MUST in possibility sense = HIGH CERTAINTY based on evidence: 'He must be home — his car is here' (deduction from observation). It does NOT express raw possibility — must is for confident inference. SHALL = strong intention/commitment ('I shall return'), older usage for future with first person. WOULD = conditional/hypothetical ('it would rain if there's enough humidity'). EXAM-FAVOURITE distinction: MAY vs MIGHT — 'may' is slightly stronger possibility; 'might' is more tentative. In conditional or past contexts, 'might' is preferred: 'If you had asked, I might have helped'. PYQ FREQUENCY: possibility-modal Qs in CGL, IBPS, RRB English 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Identify the correct modal: 'Students ___ submit their assignments by Friday.' (advice/recommendation)
questions.explanation: SHOULD = advice, recommendation, expectation. 'Students should submit by Friday' = recommended deadline. SHOULD vs MUST: 'should' is SOFTER, suggests it's a good idea but not strictly enforced; 'must' is MANDATORY, no exceptions. SHOULD also expresses: (1) Expectation: 'The bus should arrive at 9' (expected time). (2) Probability: 'Sleep should help your headache'. (3) Hypothetical past: 'You should have called me' (criticism for not doing). OUGHT TO = synonym of should but more FORMAL. 'Students ought to submit by Friday' — same meaning, more polished. NEAR-EQUIVALENTS to 'should': 'had better' (slightly stronger warning); 'are advised to' (more formal). KEY EXAM TIP: when the sentence implies ADVICE, SUGGESTION, or MILD OBLIGATION, choose SHOULD. When it implies STRICT OBLIGATION, choose MUST. PYQ FREQUENCY: should/must distinction is a SSC CGL, IBPS Clerk top-3 grammar MCQ — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Choose the modal: 'You ___ have told me earlier — now it is too late.' (regret about past)
questions.explanation: 'SHOULD HAVE + past participle' — expresses REGRET or CRITICISM about a past action that DIDN'T happen. 'You should have told me earlier' = you didn't tell me, and that was wrong. STRUCTURE: SUBJECT + SHOULD + HAVE + V3 (past participle). PARALLEL FORMS: (1) 'COULD HAVE + V3' = past possibility/missed opportunity ('I could have studied harder'). (2) 'WOULD HAVE + V3' = past hypothetical ('I would have helped if I'd known'). (3) 'MIGHT HAVE + V3' = past low-possibility ('she might have left already'). (4) 'MUST HAVE + V3' = past deduction with high confidence ('he must have forgotten'). KEY ERROR: students often write 'You should told me' (missing 'have') — incorrect; modal-perfect REQUIRES auxiliary 'have'. NEGATIVE: 'shouldn't have' = criticizing what someone DID do ('you shouldn't have spent so much'). PYQ FREQUENCY: modal-perfect (modal + have + V3) is a top SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains MCQ — 1-2× per paper.

questions.stem: Pick the correct modal: 'I ___ rather have tea than coffee.' (preference)
questions.explanation: 'WOULD RATHER' = expression of PREFERENCE, equivalent to 'prefer'. 'I would rather have tea than coffee' = 'I prefer tea to coffee'. STRUCTURE: SUBJECT + WOULD RATHER + BASE VERB. CONTRACTED FORM: I'd rather, you'd rather, etc. CHOICE-COMPARISON: 'I would rather X than Y' (X is preferred). PARALLEL EXPRESSIONS: (1) 'I prefer X to Y' (formal). (2) 'I'd prefer X' (slightly less direct than 'would rather'). (3) 'I'd sooner X' (synonym of 'would rather', slightly informal). DOUBLE-SUBJECT FORM: when expressing what you wish OTHER people would do, use PAST TENSE: 'I would rather YOU CAME on time' (you tend to be late, and I wish you'd change). KEY ERROR: students sometimes write 'I would rather to have tea' — INCORRECT (no 'to'); should be 'I would rather HAVE tea'. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'would rather' constructions appear in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English — 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests idiomatic-modal mastery.
